1:
The heading about the men of Hezekiah sets the voices looking for the history behind it. Keil and Delitzsch make Hezekiah the Jewish Pisistratos in his concern for the national literature, and his men the counterparts of those who gathered the poems of Homer; they note that the abbreviated form of the king’s name does not favour deriving the title from the collectors themselves, and that the verb rendered copied means to snatch away or transfer, so that whence they took the proverbs remains open, one rabbinic source answering from the Apocrypha, one modern scholar from the mouths of the people. Charles Ellicott supposes they had existed partly by oral tradition and partly in writing until Hezekiah had them copied into one collection; to the same care, he adds, we probably owe two books of the Psalter, and this collection holds proverbs the earlier compiler seems not to have known. Adam Clarke reports that in his old manuscript Bible this verse closes the preceding chapter, dates the collecting some two hundred and seventy years after Solomon’s death, and argues that the men of Hezekiah may have been Isaiah and Shebna, since none but inspired men could have joined such a supplement.

Matthew Henry canvasses the same question and leaves it open, whether the work fell to the prophets living then, to men trained in their schools, to priests and Levites, or to the princes of state; if it was done by the officers remembered from that reign, he says, it was no diminution to their character. He observes that Christ is greater than Solomon here, since if all he said and did were recorded the world could not contain the books. John Gill notes that some reckon a third and some a fourth part of the book to begin here, and John Wesley that many of these are political precepts concerning Hezekiah and other princes.

The glory of concealing and the honour of searching are divided between God and kings. Gill takes the concealed things for what God keeps to himself, the manner of what he reveals remaining hidden. Henry adds that his way is in the sea, so that we see what he does without knowing the reasons, and reports a reading that refers the concealment to the sins of men, since to cover sin is to pardon it. On the king’s side he requires a prince to search out the matters brought before him, examine offenders himself and not judge hastily or leave the work to others. Clarke reads it of the manner in which God publishes his will, which must be seriously studied and is the more prized when discovered, prophecy remaining dark till its accomplishment; and he breaks off to quote a letter from a royal correspondent on the divine origin of the sacred volumes. Ellicott puts it from the other end, that the further we search into nature or revelation the more depths appear, so that a man may not measure himself with his Maker.

On the unsearchable heart of kings the voices converge. Keil and Delitzsch call it a proverb of the kind that heaps up subjects before one predicate, and take the third, the heart of kings, as the point; it warns against the delusion of being flattered by a king’s favour, which may be withdrawn unawares. Ellicott says the same, and Clarke reduces it to reasons of state, which the common people can no more fathom than the height of the heavens. At the dross Keil and Delitzsch trace the words for separating and for the goldsmith; Henry makes wicked men the dross of a nation and the reformation of the court the way to that of the kingdom; Clarke says no nation has a king for a public blessing till bad counsellors are banished; and Ellicott renders the line as a vessel resulting to the refiner, who can now make one.
5:
Removing the wicked from the king finishes the figure of the refiner. John Gill assigns the parts, the wicked counsellors the dross, the king the refiner and the kingdom the silver vessel that comes out the better for their removal; Charles Ellicott adds that violence and wrong pull a throne down where righteousness establishes it.

The counsel not to push forward at court is taken as manners and morals together. Keil and Delitzsch render it as a warning not to display oneself before the king nor approach the place of the great, who by descent and office hold a lofty place in court and state; the reflexive verb, they explain, means to play the part of a person of distinction. Matthew Henry answers the charge that religion destroys good manners: it teaches a man to behave lowly towards superiors and keep his distance, not vying with them in apparel, furniture, gardens or retinue, which affronts them and wastes his own estate. He presses past manners to self-denial, that a man not covet a fair show nor thrust himself among those above him but be content in his own sphere; and this, he observes, is in fact the way to advancement, as a parable of our Saviour that seems borrowed from this verse shows, though modesty must not be pretended and made a stratagem for courting honour. Gill says a man should not appear too gay at court or make a show above his station, since princes do not love to be equalled and much less excelled. John Wesley reduces it to not affecting familiar society with greater persons, and Ellicott points to the prince whose place a man has shamelessly taken.

Adam Clarke answers the verse with eight lines of Ovid. Why, the poet asks, did Daedalus wing his way safely while his son fell and gave a sea his name, when both had the same wings? Because the son flew aloft and the father skimmed the ground. He who has lived hidden has lived well, and a man should keep below his fortune, live without envy and take his friendships among his equals. Clarke’s own counsel matches it: affect no high things, and let the desperate climb precipices.

Going to law is discouraged by all, and by Clarke with feeling. Henry says a man should not send for a writ in a passion or on the first appearance of right on his side, since we are partial in our own cause, and should weigh the certain expense against the uncertain success; he should first try to end the matter privately, as a war that must end at last might better have been prevented by a treaty. Gill asks the same beforehand, whether the cause is right, whether it will be thought vexatious, and whether the man can bear the expense. Clarke calls the law a bottomless deep to be kept from unless the direst necessity urges, observes that after a man has squandered his money on lawyers both they and the judge leave the matter to twelve of his fellow citizens, and quotes from a biography a list of eight things such a man should have: a good cause, a good purse, a skilful attorney, good evidence, able counsel, an upright judge, an intelligent jury, and good luck, without which he will probably miscarry.

On keeping another man’s secret out of the quarrel the voices agree. Wesley warns that contention must not provoke a man to divulge secrets committed to his trust, and Ellicott offers two senses, the private dealing our Lord enjoins with a brother who has wronged one, or a rule against dragging others in by disclosing their secrets. Keil and Delitzsch leave two questions undecided, whether the word for strife is an infinitive or a noun, and whether the going out is to the gate where justice was done or to the meeting with the adversary.
10:
The shame that follows a betrayed secret falls two ways. John Gill notes that either the man whose secret was told or the man told it may shame the teller, the one by publishing secrets of his own, the other by fixing on him the character of a whisperer; Charles Ellicott and John Wesley keep to the infamy that does not depart.

The word fitly spoken sets four voices on tableware. Gill renders it literally as a word spoken on its wheels, well circumstanced as to matter, time and persons, and notes that many versions make it simply seasonable. Adam Clarke applies the same figure to conversation: such a word comes in naturally, is not forced nor dragged in, and though it bears on one point will seem to suit the whole company. He then describes the vessel: the silver filigree of the East, which he has seen and calls exquisitely beautiful, is worked into flowers with the joins soldered so delicately as to be scarcely perceptible; the golden fruit showing through it, he says, pleases the eye as the fruit does the palate in a sultry climate. Matthew Henry offers golden balls resembling apples, or apples of a golden colour, set in a silver network basket through which they could be seen, and supposes it a table ornament then well known. Ellicott suggests pomegranates, citrons or oranges, and takes the pictures of silver for figured baskets.

The earring divides Clarke from the others. Keil and Delitzsch allow that the word elsewhere means a ring for the nose but hold that here, with three old versions, it means an earring; they add a scholar’s argument that the word was dropped from later usage as belonging to idol worship. Clarke makes it the nose-ring with its pendants, the left nostril pierced and a ring put through as in the ear, common, he says, in the East among women of condition. Keil and Delitzsch make the pairing the point, the two ornaments forming one ensemble as a wise reprover and a hearing ear do; Henry says the same of the transaction, that a reproof well given and well taken becomes them both. Gill observes that a golden earring gives pain when first put on and is ornamental only when well fixed.

The cold of snow in harvest is explained by three voices and doubted by one. Keil and Delitzsch deny that a snowfall is meant, which in harvest would be a calamity, and make it drink cooled with snow from the mountain clefts, where peasants near Damascus still store the winter’s snow and carry it down in summer. Ellicott says the same, supposing the use familiar to a king with a summer palace there. Clarke knows the snow-houses dug underground, but objects that stored snow was for a few only; he prefers a coldness like snow got by evaporation, wine being cooled by a wet cloth wrapped round the bottle and hung in the sun, and thinks this removes all difficulty. Henry takes the messenger rather than the drink: the meanest servant owes faithfulness to the man who sent him, and those who act by commission should act as carefully as for themselves.

The false gift is a promise unkept. Keil and Delitzsch refuse the sense of a worthless gift boasted of, since a lying promise obtains no gift at all, and note an Arabic word uniting both halves of the proverb, meaning both a boaster and a cloud that thunders much and rains little. Henry describes the man who raises expectations of what he will do for his country and what legacies he will leave, with nothing to give; Gill turns it on teachers who boast of gifts they have not; Clarke calls it a lying gift, promised and never bestowed; Ellicott and Wesley keep to the clouds, which commonly bring rain and here bring none.
15:
Patience and a soft tongue open a group on moderation here. Keil and Delitzsch make the man persuaded a judge or high officer rather than a great person, and take the verb as winning over, not deluding; long-suffering is a calmness which makes it plain in the end that the accused has right on his side, boisterous passion injuring even a just cause. Matthew Henry gives the two means separately, patience to bear a present heat without being put into a heat by it, since what is just now will be just another time, and mildness, a soft tongue mollifying the roughest spirits like the lightning said to have broken a bone without piercing the flesh. Hard words break no bones, he says, but soft words do. John Gill observes that a prince yields to patience what he would reject if it were pressed with heat, and Adam Clarke sets it beside the saying that a soft answer turns away wrath.

Honey is allowed and limited. Keil and Delitzsch call it wholesome and therefore to be eaten sparingly, and collect two sayings, a Greek line that honey taken immoderately is as bitter as gall and an old rhyme that its sweetness offends whoever takes too much. Henry allows it as no forbidden fruit, enough being as good as a feast, adding that we surfeit soonest on what is sweetest, and that the pleasures of sense turn nauseous by excess, as honey sours in the stomach. Charles Ellicott notes that finding honey was common where wild bees swarmed in the woods, whence the phrase about a land flowing with it. John Wesley extends it to all worldly delights and Clarke to all enjoyments.

The visit is limited the same way. Keil and Delitzsch quote an Arabic proverb that if your comrade eats honey you should not lick it up, render the line as making one’s foot rare at the door, and observe that love between friends may turn to hatred through too much intercourse. Henry makes it manners and wisdom not to visit too often, not to stay too long, not to come at meal-time and not to meddle in a family’s affairs, since by these he makes himself burdensome and destroys the friendship he meant to improve; he adds two Latin tags, that after three days fish and company grow distasteful and that one should be intimate with nobody, and closes by making God the better friend, whose house we need not withdraw from. Clarke says only that too much familiarity breeds contempt, and Gill that a man should make his foot rare there.

The false witness is an armoury. Keil and Delitzsch call his first line a collection of instruments of murder and the second a subscription written under it: what those weapons do is done by the false witness, who ruins his neighbour’s estate, takes away his honour and murders him. Henry sorts the three, a maul to knock a man’s brains out, a sword to wound near at hand and an arrow at a distance, and observes that a false testimony ruins not only reputation but life and estate. Ellicott glosses the maul as a hammer, connecting the word with the Latin and English names for a mallet.

The broken tooth is read two ways. Henry gives both, the confidence of an unfaithful man, whose policy and interest fail him when trouble comes, and confidence in such a man, which proves not useless only but painful, like a broken tooth or a foot out of joint that fails under a weight and hurts as it fails; Gill offers the same pair, and adds that a man who trusts his riches or his own righteousness trusts what is deceitful. Keil and Delitzsch spend their note on the form of the word broken, rejecting several scholars’ proposals, one taking it as an adjective and another emending the vowels.
20:
Songs sung to a heavy heart stand beside two other misplaced things. Keil and Delitzsch say all three are wrong, and the third morally so, since one ought to weep with those who weep, and the man who laughs among mourners is at best a fool. Matthew Henry makes the practical point: the sorrowful are comforted by sympathy, and it adds to their grief to see friends so little concerned. He notes a contrary reading, by which the garment warms and the vinegar dissolves, so that songs of comfort refresh a mourner instead of vexing him.

Adam Clarke gives the chemistry. The substance is the natron of the ancients, carbonate of soda, found as an efflorescence on the soil and in solution in certain lakes; its name comes from a root meaning to dissolve, since a solution of it takes out spots and is used in the East for washing. Pour vinegar on it and a strong fermentation follows, which is his point: between songs and a heavy heart there is no affinity, and any attempt to unite them produces opposition and strife. Charles Ellicott says the vinegar renders the nitre useless, John Wesley that it makes it ineffectual.

Feeding an enemy is no new commandment. Henry observes that the duty of loving enemies was an old commandment before our Saviour gave it fresh force by his own example, and that the way to turn an enemy into a friend is to act towards him in a friendly manner, mollifying him as a refiner melts metal by heaping coals upon it. Clarke takes the same figure from smelting and quotes four lines on the artist who melts sullen lead ore by heaping coals on its head, until the pure silver runs out below. Keil and Delitzsch commend the Greek rendering, which an apostle cites; but they refuse the common explanation that the coals stand for burning shame, since shame burns on the cheeks and not on the head, and report two scholars who take it otherwise. Ellicott keeps the shame and adds that bringing a sinner to repentance pleases God, better than a resentment that usurps his prerogative and hardens the offender. John Gill guards it likewise: the coals are not to increase the man’s punishment but to bring him to shame and repentance.

The north wind divides the voices sharply. Clarke prefers the marginal reading that the north wind brings forth rain, which he says holds at that city because the wind carries the vapours of the sea lying north of it, with three versions in support though another reads the south wind. Ellicott also thinks the margin more correct, but notes an apparent contradiction elsewhere, so that some understand the north-west; he would render the second line as a backbiting tongue causing troubled faces. Keil and Delitzsch derive the name of the north from a root meaning to conceal, from the darkening of the sky, but object that in that country the fathers of rain are the west and south-west, so that the pure north wind can hardly be meant, and note the substitutions by which older translators escaped the difficulty. Gill quotes a geographer for the north wind driving away the moist clouds. Henry leaves the weather for the moral: slanders would not be so readily spoken if they were not readily heard, and a slanderer would be silenced if he saw that his tales displeased the company, so that where we cannot otherwise reprove we may reprove by our looks.

The brawling woman is a repetition, as Keil and Delitzsch note. Henry adds that those unequally yoked are to be pitied, husband and wife alike, since it is better to be alone than joined to one who hinders the comfort of life; and those who live in solitude, wanting the comfort of society, are at least free from its vexation.
25:
Good news from a far country is valued for its rarity. Charles Ellicott says the proverb suggests how little communication passed in old times between distant countries, and John Wesley that such news is welcome because it comes rarely and after long expectation. Matthew Henry allows the desire but checks it, since bad news will come too soon and good news is welcome whenever it comes; and he turns the figure upward, heaven being a country afar off from which good news reaches us in the gospel. John Gill makes the thirsty man a traveller in hot countries where a spring is rare, and Keil and Delitzsch note that the word for thirsty properly means to be darkened, and so to faint.

The righteous man falling before the wicked is read in several ways. Keil and Delitzsch compare the righteous to a well for the blessing that flows from him, and allow the yielding to be either forced or spontaneous, most interpreters thinking of compulsion and one of a man driven from his dwelling. Henry distinguishes three cases: the righteous falling into sin where the wicked can see it; the righteous oppressed and thrust into obscurity, which troubles the fountains of justice; and the righteous turning cowardly and giving way, which reflects on religion and strengthens the hands of sinners. Ellicott takes the third: the mouth of the righteous was called a well of life, but a man who gives up his principles through fear or favour can no longer counsel out of a pure heart, and becomes a fountain fouled by the cattle that drink at it. Wesley makes it a public calamity, the state of a commonwealth whose righteous men are oppressed being as deplorable as if its fountains were corrupted.

The verse about honey and glory defeats everybody, and they say so. Keil and Delitzsch declare that as it stands it is scarcely to be understood, and then canvass four renderings and reject them all: that to set a limit to the glory of man is true glory, which the grammar will not bear; that searching out their difficulty is itself a trouble; and that the investigation of their excellence is glorious. Ellicott calls the sense very doubtful, offers that searching into difficult matters may be an honour, and sets self-indulgence against study. Adam Clarke quotes two old English versions, both making the man who will search out high things find them too heavy for him, and concludes that he who searches too far into mysteries is likely to be confounded by them; then he refuses to puzzle himself or his reader with the discordant explanations that have been offered. Henry keeps the received sense and makes it two deaths to die, to the pleasures of sense and to the praise of man, since the glory so courted is no true honour; but he reports the other reading too, that searching into glorious things is a commendation in which we cannot offend by excess. Gill says simply that too much of anything is bad, and Wesley that seeking applause industriously is not only sinful but shameful.

The city without walls closes the chapter. Keil and Delitzsch explain that such a city is one whose wall is broken, by breaches or altogether, and either way incapable of defence, so that it may be plundered without trouble; so with a man who cannot hold his desires in check. Henry sets out the good character first, a man who governs his thoughts and desires and resentments; the man without that rule breaks out into exorbitant passions when provoked, and all that is good goes out of him while all that is evil breaks in, which is as much a reproach to him as ruined walls are to a city. Ellicott says he is exposed to every temptation, and Gill that he sets no fence about his passions.
